svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. What each hop buys, and the limit no hop count changes
svg.desc: Three panels. The first sets out what each additional hop actually achieves: the first removes your network operator's view of destinations, the second splits knowledge between two parties, and the third and beyond add latency and failure modes for very little. The second panel explains the limit that no number of hops changes, which is that an adversary able to observe traffic entering the chain and leaving it can match the two by timing and volume, a weakness Tor's own designers state openly. The third panel lists what actually goes wrong in practice, which is nested clients fighting over routing, conflicting connection guards, and name resolution escaping the chain. A band below gives the three things that do change the answer.
svg.text: Figure 3: What Each Hop Buys, and What No Hop Count Changes
The instinct that more hops means more privacy is wrong in a specific and checkable way, and the specifics decide when to stop.

g.text: The first hop
Removes your network operator from
the picture and gives the destination
a different address.
This is most of the value, and it is
where the diminishing begins.
The second hop
Splits knowledge, so no single party
holds both halves. Genuinely useful,
and only if the two are separate
companies under separate control.
The third and beyond
Adds latency, cost and failure modes.
Adds very little else.
Watching both ends
An adversary who can see traffic go
into the chain and see traffic come
out of it can match the two by timing
and volume alone.
The contents are irrelevant. So is
the number of hops in between.
Stated openly by the people who
designed the strongest system
Tor's own documentation says it does
not claim to defend against somebody
who can observe both ends of a
connection. Nothing in this lesson
does better than Tor here.
So hops are not the answer to that.
Two clients, one routing table
Running two tunnel applications on one
machine has them competing to control
routes and name resolution.
Guidance calls this the easy method.
It is the least reliable one.
Two connection guards
Each wants to cut the network when its
own tunnel drops. Together they produce
states neither was designed for.
Name resolution escaping
The commonest silent failure, and the
one that undoes the whole arrangement
without any visible symptom.

svg.text: Three things that do change the answer, none of which is another hop

g.text: Reshaping the traffic. Cover traffic and regularised packet sizes attack the timing and volume matching directly, which is the only thing that does. Lesson 6.2, Figure 3.
Many relays with rotating circuits. Tor's design, which is a different answer to the same problem and a better tested one than any chain you assemble yourself.
Not being interesting at both ends. Compartmentalisation and account discipline decide far more than routing does, which is Module 5 arriving in a networking lesson.
And a verified single hop beats an unverified double one, because a chain you have not tested for leaks is a chain you do not know the shape of.

svg.text: Two hops from two separate companies is a coherent arrangement with a clear purpose. Three or more is usually a feeling rather than a threat model.
If you cannot say which specific party you are hiding the other half from, you have not yet found a reason for the second hop.
That sentence is the whole decision procedure, and it is shorter than any matrix.
